similar_scenes.name: La edad de oro del heavy metal
similar_scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
similar_scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
similar_scenes.desc: Weinstein divide la historia en cinco eras: erupción (1969-72), primera cristalización (1973-75), edad de oro o cristalización plena (1976-79), crecimiento (1979-83) y fragmentación en subgéneros (desde 1983). El núcleo del género es el código fijado en la edad de oro. Su sonido es poder: volumen, guitarra solista virtuosa con pedales y distorsión, solos obligatorios, bombo y un bajo amplificado que hace «pesado» al heavy y se siente en el pecho, y una voz emocional y potente (los aullidos de Plant y Halford, el tono operístico y áspero de Dio) que compite con la guitarra sin vencerla. En lo visual, logotipos angulosos, portadas negras y rojas con imágenes ominosas, ropa de calle, luego el cuero motero y desde 1980 el spandex. En las letras, dos polos: lo dionisíaco (sexo, alcohol y, sobre todo, el elogio del rock y del volumen) y el caos (diablo, infierno, monstruos, injusticia, locura, suicidio y muerte), con la noche como mediadora entre ambos. Tras la fragmentación sigue vivo como «classic metal», el puente entre lite metal y thrash.

similar_scenes.name: New Wave of British Heavy Metal
similar_scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
similar_scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
similar_scenes.desc: Explosión de bandas nuevas en Gran Bretaña entre 1979 y 1981. No hay un estilo común: cada grupo es bastante único, pero todos comparten la sensibilidad heavy, la juventud y el énfasis en lo visual. Muchos siguen la tradición; otros se especializan en un rasgo del código. Iron Maiden y Def Leppard triunfan a lo grande, Venom persiste con un público reducido y la mayoría desaparece, aunque alguno, como Diamond Head (versionado por Metallica), deja huella. De sus innovaciones rítmicas sale directamente el thrash. Con ella llega el «renacimiento» del heavy de principios de los ochenta.

similar_scenes.name: US Festival 1983 y el renacimiento del heavy
similar_scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
similar_scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
similar_scenes.desc: A principios de los ochenta la prensa rock habla de «revival» o «renacimiento» del heavy (Creem, octubre de 1980: el género «había hecho un Jesucristo»): nacen bandas en todo el mundo, las veteranas tocan para públicos mucho mayores y los medios se abren al metal. La señal más pública es el US Festival de 1983, patrocinado por Steve Wozniak: el día dedicado al heavy, con Ozzy, Judas Priest, Mötley Crüe, Scorpions, Quiet Riot, Van Halen y Triumph, reunió mucho más público que los otros dos.
similar_scenes.family: Cultura metal: público, medios y conciertos

similar_scenes.name: Heavy metal de los setenta
similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: «Born To Be Wild» de Steppenwolf acuña la expresión «heavy metal», que pasa a designar en EE UU el hard rock. Blue Oyster Cult definen el nuevo género (satanismo y serie B envueltos en riffs crudos); Aerosmith lo enlazan con el rhythm'n'blues depravado de Stones y Stooges; Kiss abrazan todos los estereotipos; AC/DC, las tripas del rock'n'roll (Back In Black); Journey y Boston, arquetipos del pop-metal; Rush reinventan el power-trio.

similar_scenes.name: La edad de oro del heavy metal
similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: El heavy metal renace en los mismos años que la new wave, aprovechando los sellos independientes: Motörhead (puente entre metal, Stooges/MC5 y punk), Judas Priest, Iron Maiden, Diamond Head, Def Leppard y, en EE UU, Van Halen. Entre 1982 y 1985 el subgénero gótico se convierte en «black metal» (Venom, Mercyful Fate, Celtic Frost, Helloween, Bathory). El pop-metal y el shock-rock (Twisted Sister, Mötley Crüe, Joan Jett, Bon Jovi, Savatage); la pompa y el doom (Manowar, Voivod, Saint Vitus, Pentagram); el metal progresivo (Living Colour, Queensrÿche, King's X, Pantera, Joe Satriani) y el «street sound» de Los Ángeles (Guns N' Roses, Jane's Addiction, Faster Pussycat).

podcast.title: William S. Burrows' Literary Usage (1961-1965)
podcast.body: Writer and poet William S. Burrows used the character "Uranian Willie, the Heavy Metal Kid" in his 1961 novel "The Soft Machine" and a 1965 spoken word performance. While the term appeared, Burrows was discussing aliens and addictive drugs, not music, and thus his work is not considered the origin of the musical genre's name. "Burrows isn't talking about music at all. He's actually talking about aliens and addictive drugs."

srcs.episode: Rock Explainer 4

podcast.title: Birth in 1970
podcast.body: Heavy Metal was formally born in 1970 with the release of Black Sabbath's first two albums. Their sound represented a significant break from anything previously heard, setting a new benchmark for heavy music. "Estos álbumes fueron un punto de ruptura y marcaron el nacimiento del Jebi metal."

srcs.episode: El DOOM METAL es el DARK SOULS de la música

podcast.title: Birth through Devil's Triad (1970)
podcast.body: Heavy metal is often considered by some to have originated in 1970 with Black Sabbath's debut album and title track. This birth was characterized by Tony Iomi's distinctive use of the tri tone—a flattened fifth played with a trill and distortion—an adaptation inspired by Gustav Holst's "Mars, the Bringer of War." "For some, this is the birth of heavy metal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 5: The Satanic Panic

podcast.title: Early Print Musical Reference (1970)
podcast.body: The earliest verified print reference to "heavy metal" in a musical context appeared on February 7, 1970, in Cream Magazine. Music critic Lester Bangs described The Guess Who as "heavy metal robots," though this was intended as an insult rather than a definitive genre label. "They're quite refreshing in the wake of all the heavy metal robots of the year past."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Explainer 4

podcast.title: "Cleansing Dervish" and "Shock Treatment" Description (1978)
podcast.body: Gary Mullenx, writing for the Morning News in Wilmington, Delaware in 1978, provided an evocative description of heavy metal, stating it "swirls through the mind like a cleansing dervish and wrenches the gut like a good shock treatment." This highlights the genre's intense, cathartic, and physically impactful effect on listeners. "quote, swirls through the mind like a cleansing dervish and wrenches the gut like a good shock treatment."

srcs.episode: Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal
Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal

podcast.title: 1978-1982 Music Industry Revolution
podcast.body: Between 1978 and 1982, the music industry underwent a revolution, characterized by the emergence of new forms of heavy metal. "nacían nuevas maneras de heavy metal"

srcs.episode: Cómo Michael Jackson hizo el disco más vendido de la historia

podcast.title: "Pornography of Pop" Criticism (1980)
podcast.body: In 1980, Eric Siegel penned a scathing article for the Baltimore Sun titled "Heavy Metal is the Porno of Pop," claiming the genre possessed "no redeeming social value." Siegel criticized heavy metal bands like Van Halen, Judas Priest, and Ted Nugent for sounding identical, lacking originality, and being misogynistic. "heavy metal stands as the hardcore pornography of popular music. No redeeming social value."

srcs.episode: Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal
Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal

podcast.title: Ozzy Osbourne's 1982 World Tour Promotion
podcast.body: An advertisement for Ozzy Osbourne's 1982 World Tour promised an "awesome garage of sound and light" that would "rip through you in a rage of heavy metal fury," showcasing the genre's aggressive appeal. "an awesome garage of sound in light will rip through you in a rage of heavy metal fury."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Weird History of Concert Tickets Part 1

podcast.title: Initial Lack of Soundgarden Recognition (1991)
podcast.body: In early 1991, during the filming of *Singles*, Soundgarden's *Louder Than Love* album, despite being on a major label, did not register significantly "outside the metal community." This indicates that even within heavy music subgenres, the broader appeal of what would become grunge was still limited. "Yes, Soundgarden had signed to a major label and had released their louder than love album, but outside the metal community, it didn't really register."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Key Alt-Rock Movie Soundtracks

podcast.title: Etymological Research (2013)
podcast.body: The origin of the term "heavy metal" when applied to music was extensively researched by Dina Weinstein, a professor of sociology at DePaul University in Chicago. In 2013, she published a paper titled "Just So Stories, How Heavy Metal Got Its Name, A Cautionary Tale," attempting to solve this etymological puzzle by examining various sources. "She wrote a paper entitled Just So Stories, How Heavy Metal Got Its Name, A Cautionary Tale."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Explainer 4

podcast.title: "Near Death" in Late 1970s and 1980s Decline
podcast.body: Heavy metal experienced a "near death" period in the late 1970s, largely due to the dominance of disco, a "dance music wave that nearly crushed everything in its path." While it achieved immense popularity in the 1980s, this ubiquity eventually led to fan burnout (except among the most loyal) and a decline in popularity by the late 80s, as it ceased to feel rebellious. "this was a you know a dance music wave that nearly crushed everything in its path until disco died out in fact in some ways heavy metal in the 80s followed the same path as disco it became so popular that all but most of the loyalist fans kind of got burned out on it and if it's not rebellious anymore."

srcs.episode: Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal
Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal

podcast.title: "Satanic Messaging" Controversy
podcast.body: A significant and persistent criticism, particularly directed at Black Sabbath, involved the genre's "so-called satanic messaging." Despite bands denying outright satanic affiliations, this perception contributed to heavy metal's controversial and intimidating image. "certainly one of the criticisms of heavy metal, especially lobbied at or lobbed, I should say, at black Sabbath, is the so-called satanic messaging."

srcs.episode: Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal
Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal

podcast.title: "You Really Got Me" - First Heavy Metal Claim
podcast.body: The Kinks' song "You Really Got Me" has been "often been called the first heavy metal record." It is credited with introducing records dominated by heavy distorted guitar riffs to the top of the UK charts, marking a significant moment in the genre's nascent development. "Today we're going to look at a record that has often been called the first heavy metal record, one that introduced records dominated by heavy distorted guitar riffs to the top of the UK charts."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 119: "You Really Got Me" by the Kinks

podcast.title: Audience Transformation and Mainstreaming
podcast.body: Heavy metal's audience underwent a significant transformation from the early to mid-1980s. Initially the music of "misunderstood teenagers," its reach expanded far beyond its subcultural roots to embrace suburban audiences, shifting from "dark" to "party music, fun music, loud and fun." Author Chuck Klosterman noted that metal began telling alienated kids they were "not different at all," but rather "hyper normal," "extremely popular," and "totally cool." "instead of telling an alienated kid that it was okay to be different metals seem to say that you're not different at all in fact your hyper normal in fact your extremely popular and totally cool."

Ep. 54 - Into the 80s! What Came Next for 70s Heavy Metal

podcast.title: Band T-Shirt Concert Etiquette
podcast.body: Metal fans are often noted for proudly wearing shirts of the bands on the bill when attending a gig, a practice compared to wearing a home team's jersey at a sporting event. "Metal fans will often go to a gig proudly representing the bands of the bill by wearing one of their shirts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Survey Says: Useful and Odd Music Surveys and Polls

podcast.title: Band T-Shirt Ownership Statistics
podcast.body: Metal fans own the most band t-shirts, with an average of 10 shirts per fan, and also spend the most on such gear, dropping $500 or more over their lives on t-shirts. "Metal fans, and there they are again, own the most banned t-shirts with an average of 10."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Survey Says: Useful and Odd Music Surveys and Polls

podcast.title: Class and Age Divisions in Audience
podcast.body: Heavy metal found its audience across specific class and age demographics, primarily appealing to lower and lower-middle class youth, as well as high school students over college students. Historically and critically, it's largely considered the domain of the "white working class young male," who often resisted critics' claims that the music lacked lyrical depth. "Heavy metal spoke to class and age divisions in the audience, lower and lower middle class versus bourgeois and college students versus high school students."

srcs.episode: Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal
Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal

podcast.title: Component of Trap Metal
podcast.body: Heavy metal is identified as a core component of the Trap Metal genre, blending with trap music to create this hybrid sound. "this genre brings together trap music, a type of hip hop that came out of Atlanta and heavy metal"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 3: The New Genres

podcast.title: Critical Reception vs. Fan Loyalty (70s/80s)
podcast.body: In the 1970s and early 1980s, what would become known as heavy metal (initially called hard rock) was met with significant disdain from rock critics. However, it was adored by its loyal fan base, predominantly young white males, who often came from lower to middle-class socio-economic backgrounds, highlighting a clear class division in rock appreciation. "As the 80s begin critics still do not think much of heavy metal radio has been taken over by corporations that continue to ignore heavy metal this time in favor of new wave acts like Durant Iran, the go goes arena rock like sticks, journey. And fans of heavy metal still could not care less if you liked their music or not it was still true that heavy metal bands owed their existence to the fans who went to their live shows, bought their t-shirts and really did not give a shit what critics thought in fact so much the better if heavy metal was not on Casey casem's American top 40."

Ep. 54 - Into the 80s! What Came Next for 70s Heavy Metal

podcast.title: Cultural Identity Parallel
podcast.body: Heavy Metal is referenced as a genre, similar to punk, that successfully established music as a cultural identity, a form of belonging, and resistance. This idea was later consolidated by Gabber for electronic dance music. "al igual que el panc, el heavy metal, también podía ser una identidad, una forma de pertenencia y resistencia."

podcast.title: Dating Preferences Impact
podcast.body: A study on driving and dating revealed that 28% of women considered metal to be a "turn off." "Meanwhile, 28% of women said that metal was a turn off."

podcast.title: Debate Over Coining the Term
podcast.body: The origin of the term "heavy metal" remains a subject of debate among music historians and critics. Possible coiners include legendary rock critic Lester Bangs (portrayed by Philip Seymour Hoffman in *Almost Famous*), author William Burrows in his novel *Naked Lunch*, or Mars Bonfire, who wrote the Steppenwolf classic "Born to Be Wild" which contains the lyric "heavy metal thunder." "Was it the legendary rock critic Lester bangs who you might recall being portrayed by the great Philip Seymour Hoffman in the movie almost famous? Was it the author William Burrows and naked lunch? Was it Mars Bonfire who wrote the Steppenwolf classic born to be wild you know heavy metal thunder?"

Ep. 54 - Into the 80s! What Came Next for 70s Heavy Metal

podcast.title: Debate on Origins
podcast.body: There is a debate regarding the exact start of heavy metal. Some consider the "heavy sound" of bands like Led Zeppelin or Deep Purple in the late 1960s as its beginning, while others (like the speaker) mark the official start with Black Sabbath in 1970 due to their introduction of a full aesthetic and thematic framework beyond just sound. "hay quien considera el inicio del heavy metal el sonido heavy que empieza ya con lecepeling o con diparpo en las finales de los 60."

srcs.episode: Black Sabbath: Y así nació el HEAVY METAL

podcast.title: Defining Characteristics
podcast.body: Heavy metal is defined not only by a specific way of playing and tuning instruments but also by an overarching thematic and aesthetic approach. This comprehensive identity became a foundational characteristic of the movement. "no solo es esa manera de tocar voy a manera de afinar los instrumentos sino que toda una temática y toda una estética."

srcs.episode: Black Sabbath: Y así nació el HEAVY METAL

podcast.title: Defining Musical Elements
podcast.body: Heavy metal is defined by its loud and aggressive musical characteristics, including loud vocals, thundering drum beats, crunchy power chords, and distorted electric guitars. These very elements, often scorned by critics, were precisely what resonated with its fanbase. The incorporation of taboo, satanic, or mystic symbolism further amplified its appeal to young, rebellious audiences. "What we can all agree on is that this is loud, aggressive music, and the very things that the critics hated, the loud vocals, the thundering drum beat, the crunchy power cord, the distorted electric guitar, that's exactly what its fans liked."

srcs.episode: Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal
Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal

podcast.title: Early History Focus
podcast.body: The discussion focuses significantly on the origins and early history of heavy metal, specifically prior to 1980, with bands like Black Sabbath, Led Zeppelin, Motörhead (briefly mentioned but not elaborated), and Deep Purple being key figures in its development. "heavy metal anterior a 1980 tengo un montón no tengo mucho moderno pero cplim, black Sabbath, motoged y todos en keys todos estos grupos tan importantes en los inicios del heavy metal así que los tengo."

srcs.episode: Black Sabbath: Y así nació el HEAVY METAL

podcast.title: Early Roots of Complexity
podcast.body: The roots of heavy metal, exemplified by bands like Led Zeppelin, also contributed to the era when rock was becoming more complex and elaborate. "justo también la raíces del heavy metal, venía los discos de la Ecépeling, el roque se había convertido en música muy compleja, muy elaborada, muy barroca, a veces un poco engreída, veces un poco pretenciosa."

podcast.title: Early Sexual and Masculine Sound (1970s)
podcast.body: The nascent heavy metal genre in the 1970s, exemplified by bands like Led Zeppelin and songs such as "Whole Lotta Love," introduced a distinctive "sexual and masculine and dominating" sound to music, pushing new boundaries of expression. "this song not only is giving a glimpse into the beginning of heavy metal, but we are getting it in a way that is very sexual and masculine and dominating."

Ep. 4 - Music of the 70s (Sexual) Revolution

podcast.title: Early Terminology - "Hard Rock"
podcast.body: Upon its emergence, the genre now recognized as heavy metal was initially referred to as "hard rock." The term "heavy metal" itself did not exist in musical discourse at that time, highlighting the evolving nature of genre classification. "What we now know as heavy metal was usually referred to as hard rock."

Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal

podcast.title: Emergence as Genre Descriptor (Mid-1970s)
podcast.body: The term "heavy metal" entered the music vernacular in the mid-1970s, gaining widespread use to describe a new wave of "loud, heavy guitar rock." This sound was pioneered by bands like Led Zeppelin, Black Sabbath, and Deep Purple, solidifying "heavy metal" as one of rock's most significant subgenres. "By the mid-1970s, everybody was using it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Explainer 4

podcast.title: Emergence from Early Rock Bands
podcast.body: Heavy Metal originated from the foundational elements laid by early rock bands, with groups like The Jarpers being a key "seed" for its development. The disintegration and subsequent offshoots of these initial bands directly contributed to the birth of new genres. "De esas trizas nacería la psicodelia nacería el heavy metal inatadía nacería muchísimas cosas."

srcs.episode: The Yardbirds, una banda clave para entender la historia de la música

podcast.title: Enhanced Wood Consumption by Termites
podcast.body: Studies have indicated that termites consume wood at double the rate when exposed to heavy metal music. "Germites will eat wood two times faster if they're exposed to heavy metal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Useless information

podcast.title: Epic Fantasy Stories
podcast.body: Heavy metal is recognized for its tradition of epic fantasy stories. The second story on "Marderoth de Universe" by King Gisart and Elisar Wysart, "Lord of Light y versus Balrog," is noted for its potential to fit this genre if it were more detailed and coherent. "Esas historias épicas del heavy metal, un poco más de fantasía."

srcs.episode: King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard: ¿Pero que significa Murder of the Universe?

podcast.title: Fan Defense - Escapism and Working-Class Identity
podcast.body: In a fervent response to critics like Eric Siegel, fans defended heavy metal as a form of fantasy and escapism, likened to John Wayne movies or comic books. Keith Cunningham of Edgewood, Maryland, championed it as "solid working class music," describing it as "fast, unsophisticated and to the point," and crucially, as providing "anthems to teenhood and teenage frustration," accurately conveying "the screaming nerves of pubescent frustration." "Heavy metal is a fantasy worked out on stage just as much as John Wayne movies, comic books and pinball machines. Heavy metal is a way of escaping the doldrums of everyday life, nothing more than nothing less."

srcs.episode: Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal
Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal

podcast.title: Fan Loyalty and Disregard for Critics
podcast.body: Heavy metal fans are characterized by their exceptional loyalty and indifference to critical disapproval, often embracing negative reviews as a positive "feature." This fervent dedication, manifest in record purchases, concert attendance, and merchandise buying, was fundamental to sustaining bands' careers, effectively telling critics to "be damned." "That music fans can be very loyal. That's especially true of heavy metal fans, and could not care less if a critic likes their music or not."

srcs.episode: Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal
Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal

podcast.title: Fans Most Likely to Run Sub-7 Minute Mile
podcast.body: A study commissioned by the website Test Fitness Equipment found that heavy metal fans are the demographic most likely to be able to run a mile in under seven minutes. "heavy metal fans are most likely to be able to run a sub seven minute mile."

podcast.title: Heavy Metal Knitting Championship (Finland)
podcast.body: The annual Heavy Metal Knitting Championship, held in Finland, requires participants to knit while performing interpretively to metal music. This unique competition continued even amidst the pandemic, with the 2021 winner, "the Knitting Witch," hailing from the Netherlands. "This requires entrance to actually knit something while performing interpretively against a backdrop of metal music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 60 Mind-Blowing Things About Music: 2021 Edition

podcast.title: Increased UK Chart Presence (2010s)
podcast.body: Heavy metal, particularly groups from indie labels, saw an increased presence on the UK charts during the 2010s. "Heavy metal and hard rock, again, groups drawn largely from indie labels, saw an increased presence on the charts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Initial Critical Reception
podcast.body: In the 1970s, heavy metal faced overwhelming disdain from rock critics, with virtually no positive commentary. Robert Duncan, a writer and editor for Cream Magazine, famously lambasted the genre, calling it "pimply, pearl, putrid, unsheak, unsophisticated, anti-intellectual, but impossibly pretentious, dismal, abysmal, terrible, horrible, and stupid music, barely music at all." "Heavy metal, pimply, pearl, putrid, unsheak, unsophisticated, anti-intellectual, but impossibly pretentious, dismal, abysmal, terrible, horrible, and stupid music, barely music at all."

Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal

podcast.title: Lollapalooza Purist Conflict
podcast.body: The inclusion of Metallica, a heavy metal band, on the 1996 Lollapalooza tour caused a rift with "true alternative people" who felt they did not belong, highlighting a perceived genre incompatibility within the alternative scene. "Many of the early adopters of alternative, true alternative people, felt that Metallica and their fans didn't belong."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 3: Grunge

podcast.title: Market Growth in the Mid-80s
podcast.body: Despite initial critical and radio neglect, heavy metal experienced a remarkable surge in popularity in the mid-1980s. In 1983, it accounted for only 8% of music sold, but by 1984, that figure dramatically increased to 20%. This growth signaled its transition from a subculture to a more mainstream genre, eventually leading MTV to devote an entire show, "Headbangers Ball," to it just two years later. "In 1983 only 8% of music sold was classified as heavy metal but a year later by 1984 that number jumped to 20% in two years after that MTV devoted an entire show to heavy metal called headbangers ball."

Ep. 54 - Into the 80s! What Came Next for 70s Heavy Metal

podcast.title: Moral Panic Target (1970s)
podcast.body: In the 1970s, metal music, alongside punk, significantly contributed to the moral outrage of conservatives. Critics viewed this music as corrupting youth, turning them into "rebellious, disrespectful, and anti-establishment goons," prompting calls for its immediate cessation. "Then, the metal and punk of the 1970s just got them into more of a froth. This music is turning our children into rebellious, disrespectful, and anti-establishment goons. It must be stopped."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Motivational Music for Bodybuilding
podcast.body: Heavy metal music is a popular choice for bodybuilders, with studies indicating its effectiveness in keeping them "pumped up" between sets. The loud, aggressive nature of the music is believed to contribute to sustained motivation during weight training.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Medical Mysteries of Music

podcast.title: Origin in Blues Music
podcast.body: The concept of "scary devil music," a cornerstone of early heavy metal, did not originate with bands like Black Sabbath but rather evolved from the blues. This lineage underscores the genre's deep historical roots in music that challenged conventional norms and appealed to rebellious instincts. "Like rock music itself, that came from the blues. The music your mom does not want you to hear, and so come hell or high water, you will find that music."

Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal

podcast.title: Origins from Black Sabbath's Sound
podcast.body: The distinctive sound of Black Sabbath, characterized by its heaviness, sinister quality, and power, which resulted from Tony Iommi's adaptive guitar techniques after an industrial accident, significantly contributed to the creation of heavy metal as a genre. "And the Sabbath sound went a long way to creating the sound of heavy metal as we know it today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Metal music is unsuitable for dogs because its tempo does not match their resting heartbeat. "so metal is out."

podcast.title: Proliferation of Distorted Chords (1960s-1970s)
podcast.body: The rise of heavy distorted music in the 1960s and 1970s led to a widespread proliferation of chords like the devil's tri tone. This sonic characteristic became ubiquitous, notably in songs by foundational artists such as Black Sabbath and Jimi Hendrix. "And as heavy distorted music took off in the 1960s and 70s, these kinds of chords proliferated everywhere."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 5: The Satanic Panic

podcast.title: Rebellion and Escape
podcast.body: While rebellion wasn't exclusive to heavy metal, the genre strongly resonated with the "youth revolt" and "backlash against the establishment" of the early 1970s. Even if fans didn't perceive their musical taste as overtly political, their embrace of a widely "distasteful" genre constituted a political act. Continued loyalty into adulthood is attributed to nostalgia or an ongoing search for escape, particularly against the backdrop of the turbulent 1970s marked by war, Watergate, and economic instability. "Rebellion was not at all exclusive to heavy metal and it is way too simplistic to say that that is all that there was about the music still the early 70s when heavy metal is born is this era of youth revolt a backlash against the establishment if you will."

srcs.episode: Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal
Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal

podcast.title: Reflection of 80s Culture
podcast.body: Heavy metal music in the 1980s served as a reflection of the era's cultural landscape, embodying themes of "excess," "newer, bigger, better, greed as good materialism." This intrinsic connection meant that the genre's evolution mirrored the prevailing societal values and economic trends of the time. "Music changes to reflect the era in 80s. That's the time of excess. Newer, bigger, better, greet as good materialism, all of it. And heavy metal reflected that."

srcs.episode: Ep. 54 - Into the 80s! What Came Next for 70s Heavy Metal
Ep. 54 - Into the 80s! What Came Next for 70s Heavy Metal

podcast.title: Rick Johnson's Critiques
podcast.body: Rick Johnson, a writer for *Cream* magazine, offered a vivid and often critical perspective on heavy metal throughout its evolution. In a 1979 article titled "Is Heavy Metal Dead," he described it as "rock and roll that gives your ears the urge to make voodoo dolls out of your stereo speakers" and predicted its decline, calling established bands "fumbling flyfarts." Years later, in "Heavy Metal Must Be Destroyed," he argued it was "no longer music it was a marketing strategy," reflecting its mainstream commercialization. "Heavy metal is rock and roll that gives your ears the urge to make voodoo dolls out of your stereo speakers."

Ep. 54 - Into the 80s! What Came Next for 70s Heavy Metal

podcast.title: Scientific Origin
podcast.body: The term "heavy metals" originates from chemistry and metallurgy, referring to actual metals with high densities such as iron, copper, tin, silver, gold, platinum, gallium, thallium, and hafnium. This scientific usage predates its musical application. "Heavy metals are actual metals with high densities."

podcast.body: Heavy metal finished "dead last" on playlists designed for sexual encounters, alongside classic rock. "Heavy metal and classic rock finished dead last."

podcast.title: Sexual Partners Average
podcast.body: Metal fans, on average, reported the most lifetime sexual partners among all genres surveyed, with an average of 17. This was attributed to their extroverted nature and a "zest for adventure." "In the UK, it's metal fans that on average get the most nookie with 17 partners."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sexual Preferences and Habits
podcast.body: A study found that 72% of metalheads say they have some kind of fetish, and 82% admit to having had an all-night stand. "We also learned that 72% of metalheads say that they have a fetish of some kind and 82% of them admit to having an all night stand."

srcs.episode: Survey Says: Useful and Odd Music Surveys and Polls

podcast.title: Shift Towards Speed and Virtuosity
podcast.body: After its initial emergence, Heavy Metal quickly evolved, with bands increasingly pursuing a faster, more technical sound. This trend placed a strong emphasis on virtuosity, diverging from the slower, heavier roots established by pioneers like Black Sabbath. "el metal empezaba a lezgar un sonido más rápido, técnico y orientado al virtudosismo."

srcs.episode: El DOOM METAL es el DARK SOULS de la música

podcast.title: Shift in UK Market Dominance
podcast.body: This increased chart presence marked a shift from a long period where American metal and hard rock bands, with few exceptions like Accept and Scorpions, largely dominated the British market. "And this was a nice change from a long stretch where American metal and hard rock bands pretty much had the British market to themselves, with a couple of bands like Accept and Scorpions thrown in."

podcast.title: Sound as "Evil" Appeal
podcast.body: The appeal of heavy metal, even in songs containing overtly Christian lyrics like Black Sabbath's "After Forever," is largely attributed to its sonic quality. It "sounds scary" and "sounds evil," and this inherent sound is identified as a primary source of its attraction. "it's scary because it sounds scary, and it sounds evil and therein lies the appeal."

podcast.title: Studying Effectiveness
podcast.body: Metal was identified as the second worst type of music for studying due to its distracting nature, with only 8% of respondents finding it productive. "Metal is the second worst study music, because it's also too distracting."

podcast.title: Target of Conservative Groups (1980s)
podcast.body: Heavy metal's emergence in the early 1980s prompted strong reactions from conservative parent groups, who sought government intervention to ban its radio broadcast and censor its distribution due to perceived explicit content. "ante el nacimiento de los 80 del heavy metal pusieron un grito en el cielo y quisieron hacer un acuerdo con el gobierno para prohibir su radio de difusión y sobre todo para fomentar la censura y la no distribución de ese tipo de material."

podcast.title: Technological Evolution in the 1970s
podcast.body: The genre's signature loudness and aggression were made possible by technological advancements in the 1970s, particularly the development of powerful amplifiers, pioneered by figures such as Jim Marshall. The availability of this technology was a key factor in metal's evolution. "You needed an amplifier, which is just one of the reasons that metal evolved in the 70s. The technology was there."

podcast.title: Themes of Fantasy and Escapism
podcast.body: Much like other musical genres, heavy metal served as a vehicle for fantasy and escapism, with this effect often derived more from its sound than its lyrical content. It provided a powerful release from the "doldrums of everyday life." "Like a lot of music, the genre was very much about fantasy and escapism, and that often came from the sound more than the words."

podcast.title: Transformation from Novelty Song
podcast.body: A simple novelty cowboy song, originally written for an Abbott and Costello film, underwent an "alchemy" at the hands of the Rock and Roll Trio to become a heavy metal anthem. "a novelty song about cowboys written for an Ableton Castello film became a heavy metal anthem performed by every group that ever played a distorted riff."

podcast.title: Troubadour's Shift in the 1980s
podcast.body: By the 1980s, The Troubadour transitioned to heavy metal as its primary genre. This shift was significant, leading to the discovery of bands like Guns N' Roses by figures such as David Geffen at the venue. "And in the 1980s, heavy metal is going to become the main genre of the troubadour."

podcast.title: Visceral vs. Intellectual Reaction
podcast.body: Dina Weinstein, in her scholarly analysis, concluded that heavy metal "brings out visceral rather than intellectual reactions in both its fans and detractors." This observation underscores the genre's primary impact as an emotional and gut-level experience. "heavy metal brings out visceral rather than intellectual reactions in both its fans and detractors."
